With the launch of the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro variant, Apple has quietly removed one of the most appealing features of this machine. Although the two new Mac minis look almost identical to the previous generation on the outside, Apple has taken away a hidden feature from the previous Mac mini that made it extremely good value for money.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, it was truly a remarkable bargain. It not only came with Apple's M4 SoC, but also featured 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. Priced at just US$599, with a student price of only US$499. The M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's lineup, but in terms of value for money, it was the best Mac across the entire range.

Video: Apple Killed the Mac mini's Best Hidden Feature :(

However, this smallest Mac from Apple actually had another secret weapon that made it even more worthwhile: a storage upgrade slot. Users could actually open the cover on the back of the machine, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module, making it easy to swap in a third-party SSD with capacities of up to 2TB.

The benefits of this design were multifaceted. In addition to being able to upgrade the SSD or easily repair a faulty drive, you could also save a considerable amount of money by not having to choose Apple's custom upgrade options, handling it yourself with a much cheaper third-party SSD.

Back then, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade option at US$800, and with a single click you could transform this 'budget' computer into a US$1,400 machine. But if you bought the machine and then upgraded it yourself with a third-party SSD, users could save nearly US$500.

Of course, as someone who loves tinkering, I was extremely excited about this at the time, and even made a full video tutorial demonstrating step-by-step how to upgrade the original SSD with a third-party drive. The video received a pretty good response, accumulating 500,000 views.

Video: How to Upgrade the M4 Mac mini SSD

Good things never last.

With the launch of the latest generation Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly onto the motherboard, completely剥夺ing users of the possibility of upgrading with a third-party NAND module after purchase.

The Mac mini has gone from being unquestionably the best value Mac to a considerably more expensive product, not only with the base model rising from US$600 to US$900, but the 2TB upgrade option also increasing from US$800 to US$1,000.

If you want to buy an M6 Mac mini with 2TB SSD now, you have to pay Apple US$1,900. Compared to a comparable M4 Mac mini, factoring in the after-market upgrade price of around US$320 at the time, it would only cost about US$920. Of course, everything is more expensive now, so this comparison may not be entirely fair to Apple (look how fair I am), but this is a US$1,000 increase, not only because Apple has raised prices significantly, but also because Apple has eliminated the possibility of user upgrades.

Apple raising the base Mac mini by US$300, I can roughly guess the reason, and I can also understand SSD prices rising so much. Due to AI and other factors, the prices of components, SSDs, and memory have all soared dramatically. But this does not explain why Apple had to solder the SSD onto the motherboard instead of retaining the user-replaceable design as before.

MaxM's Top Comments

They absolutely have the capability to do it, they simply choose not to. Major markets and regions like the EU, China, and India should enforce strict guidelines requiring phone manufacturers including Apple to adopt modular designs. This regulation should also extend to companies like Sony and Microsoft. Consumer protection simply does not exist right now.

We can speculate, but why Apple chose to revert to the soldered SSD design may forever remain unknown. But what we do know is that these machines are indeed considerably more expensive, and saying so might even be an understatement. Comparing an M4 Mac mini with a 2TB after-market upgrade to an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB factory upgrade, that's roughly a 106% increase.

9to5Mac's Take

Finding a reasonably priced base model M4 Mac mini on the second-hand market may be a bit difficult, but if you do manage to find one, it remains a fantastic computer, whether in terms of basic performance, features, or the upgradable SSD.

The good news is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, so you can easily add more high-bandwidth external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I'm quite fond of the Samsung T9, which is a relatively affordable way to add extra storage space.

Why do you think Apple removed the user-replaceable SSD from the Mac mini? Do you have any particular theories? Share your thoughts in the comments.
